noticias.titulo: French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler
noticias.resumen: The court has upheld the 2020 beating of the black music producer as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
noticias.texto:
French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler
- Published
Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.
Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.
Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.
Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.
All were told they could never serve in the police again.
The case became a cause cÃ©lÃ¨bre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.
Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.
This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.
Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.
The case was heard by a panel of five judges.
The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.
They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.
After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.
The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.
During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.
In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".
  - Published27 November 2020

noticias.titulo: In a year of AI solving maths problems, Anthropic may have just solved the biggest
noticias.resumen: A mathematician at Anthropic says he used an AI to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis, though verification will take some time.
noticias.texto:
In a year of AI solving maths problems, Anthropic may have just solved the biggest
- Published
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.
Levent AlpÃ¶ge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.
If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. AlpÃ¶ge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".
The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.
As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.
It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.
Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.
Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.
AlpÃ¶ge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.
"The precise timing is horrible," AlpÃ¶ge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."
"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.
The complete textual proof that AlpÃ¶ge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.
Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off.
"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.
No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.
OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.
More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.
The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.
Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external.
A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".
"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.
A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.
It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

noticias.titulo: Mamdani announces plan to close New York's Rikers Island jail by 2032
noticias.resumen: Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it but delays arose over where to place inmates.
noticias.texto:
Mamdani announces plan to close New York's Rikers Island jail by 2032
- Published
New York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new plan from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.
Mamdani on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island complex by 2032, to build four new jails and drastically reduce the city's detainee population.
Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it by this year. But plans have been delayed over the years in part due to the logistical difficulties over where to place inmates.
Dana Kaplan - who Mamdani appointed as the city's "Close Rikers Czar" told the BBC News channel on Friday that his latest proposal is not just about getting rid of a decrepit facility.
It is also a "generational opportunity" to "build a different type of detention system" and figure out how to detain people more appropriately, she said.
The Rikers Island jail complex is perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, and has earned a variety of nicknames over the years because of its dilapidated conditions, including Gladiator School and Torture Island. The jail has housed a number of high-profile inmates awaiting trial, including Tupac Shakur, DMX and Harvey Weinstein.
It houses more than 6,500 inmates at a given time. Mamdani hopes to reduce that number to 4,100 - a goal that has been met with skepticism by the New York City correction officers' union.
"[B]uilding a new system that puts an arbitrary cap on the City's available jail beds is ill-conceived, irresponsible and jeopardizes the safety of all New Yorkers, including our Officers," NYC Correction Officers' Benevolent Association said in a statement. "The City cannot keep the jail population at around 4,100 without irresponsibly releasing individuals who committed violent felony charges."
Kaplan disagreed.
"It's actually possible to have fewer people in jail in New York City - and that is what we should be planning for," she said.
The jail complex has long faced backlash over staffing shortages, crumbling conditions and inmate deaths in the facility, including nine this year. Legislation required the jail to be shuttered by 2027, but Mamdani blamed lags under former Mayor Eric Adams' administration as well as the Covid pandemic for the delays.
Last year, under Adams, a federal judge removed Rikers from the city's control, appointing an independent outside official to make decisions concerning the facility.
In an 88-page report released on Friday, Mamdani said Rikers was a product of "deteriorating infrastructure" and that officials had a "moral imperative" to close it.
New York City Council must approve the updated timeline, with members, including the city's speaker, indicating they support the plan.
Mamdani's office said the city would open up four new jails - one in Brooklyn by 2029, two in the Bronx and Queens by 2031 and one in Manhattan by 2032.
The mayor's office argues the new, smaller facilities will provide inmates "access to daylight, fresh air and clean space" leading to better outcomes for detainees. The facilities will be easier for families to access as well, as travel to the remote Rikers can take hours.
Mamdani said his administration would work to reduce the number of people being held in jail across New York City, including by offering alternative programmes to detention for some awaiting trial, by making it easier for families to post bail online and by trying to speed up the pretrial legal process.
He also wants to open up hundreds of beds in therapeutic housing units for prisoners with serious mental health issues.
Kaplan said Mamdani's administration had already opened 100 therapeutic beds at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan, moving 100 people off of Rikers Island.
The proposal involves a large investments: $146m (Â£111m) for mental health and substance use treatment and vocational and education programming inside and outside the jails.

noticias.titulo: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
noticias.resumen: The Russian embassy in Denmark has denied the allegation, which has led to Russia's defence attaché being expelled.
noticias.texto:
Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
- Published
Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.
Denmark's security and intelligence agency said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.
Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attachÃ© will now be expelled.
Russia's Embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.
In a statement posted on social media, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia".
Russian state media cites the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly".
Danish media named the target of the assassination attempt as the rapper known as Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Vasiliev.
Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said the individuals who allegedly tried to assassinate him were associated with a banned Danish gang named Loyal to Familia. The group is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity", according to the agency.
PET, which worked with police on the case, said three individuals were stopped while travelling by car near the music venue where Kyivstoner was set to perform on 25 September.
Firearms and knives were found in the vehicle, PET said.
Since then, two people linked to the case have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
Both individuals pleaded not guilty to the charges, local media reported.
In July, Russia's FSB security service accused Vasiliev and the Ukrainian authorities of organising a "terrorist attack" on military facilities and personnel in Russia. The rapper denied this allegation on social media.
In a statement on Friday, Danish Foreign Minister Lars LÃ¸kke Rasmussen said the alleged assassination attempt was Russian "intimidation" and an attempt to make Denmark "waver" in its support for Ukraine.
Russia's defence attachÃ© must leave the country within seven days, Rasmussen said.
He also said Denmark wants the EU to restrict the ability of Russians to travel throughout Europe, saying even though Denmark is already very reluctant to issue visas, Russians can still get a Schenegen visa in another country and travel to Denmark. Denmark wants these visas to apply only in the country that has issued them, he added.

noticias.titulo: US declassifies more UFO footage filmed in the Middle East
noticias.resumen: The Pentagon has released an eighth tranche of UFO records, which includes three video clips recorded in 2020, 2023 and 2026.
noticias.texto:
US declassifies more UFO footage filmed in the Middle East
The US government released an eighth tranche of records regarding Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAPs), marking the latest step in an effort to declassify government files on UFOs.
After US President Donald Trump called for UFO files to be released in an executive order earlier this year, the Pentagon has declassified hundreds of files. The first tranche was released 8 May 2026.
The footage in this video makes up three of the 43 files released in this tranche. All three clips were filmed from aboard US military platforms in the Middle East in 2020, 2023 and 2026.

noticias.titulo: What the new UK-EU deal could mean for future post-Brexit relations
noticias.resumen: The BBC's political and Europe editors analyse the new agreements between the UK and EU.
noticias.texto:
What the new UK-EU deal could mean for future post-Brexit relations
The United Kingdom and European Union reached a deal on Friday strengthening post-Brexit ties following a summit in Brussels.
The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, while European Council President AntÃ³nio Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.
The BBC's political editor Chris Mason and Europe editor Katya Adler analyse the new agreement and what it could mean for future relations between the UK and EU.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".

noticias.titulo: They were fined $811m for conning detained migrants, but the scams didn't stop
noticias.resumen: How convicted fraudsters made millions from detained immigrants, evaded efforts to shut down their bail business and left migrants behind bars.
noticias.texto:
They were fined $811m for conning detained migrants, but the scams didn't stop
- Published
Every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being detained. Her friends had paid her bail, and she wanted to look presentable when she was finally released.
But every day, she was told her bond had not been paid.
Juarez was confused. Her friends had wired $2,600 (Â£1,970) to a bond company, Libre Immigration Services (LIS), that had been recommended by her lawyer. LIS said it would begin "the process of paying her immigration bond". But the next day came, and the day after that, with no release.
What she didn't know was that LIS was owned by a convicted fraudster, who had acquired the assets of another bail company co-founded by two men who also had fraud convictions. These two men were fined $811m in 2024 for scamming their clients.
Their firm, Libre By Nexus, which was at one point the largest immigration bail company in America, had appeared to shut down after federal regulators caught up with them.
But public records and BBC interviews with clients and former employees reveal a tangle of interconnected operations continued - along with the flow of cash - while leaving immigrants stuck in detention centres.
Since President Donald Trump has returned to office after promising an immigration crackdown, Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made over 1.2m arrests, and fast-tracked deportations. The administration has tried unsuccessfully to make it illegal to give migrants bail but the sharp increase in detentions has increased demand for bond companies to secure bail and their release.
Conditions in these centres can be poor. Held in custody, away from family, often scared to speak out, many have faced health problems and endured inadequate food or treatment, according to immigrant advocates and reports by the US government.
In the detention centre where Juarez was locked up, she and about 100 other detainees slept in bunks laid out in rows in a cacophonous room. The lights were left on all night and guards routinely woke everyone up for roll call. According to Castro and advocacy groups, detainees who caused trouble were put in "the hold" - solitary confinement.
The White House and officials from Homeland Security did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
For Juarez, the wait to be bailed out of detention seemed interminable.
In an email to the BBC, a spokesperson for LIS said Juarez "misunderstands" their services - that they are not bondsmen themselves, but they connect detained individuals to those who are licensed bondsmen. They said another company ultimately decided not to work with her.
An email sent by LIS, and reviewed by the BBC, said that the company had paid a cash bond to ICE on behalf of Juarez. The message was forwarded to Juarez as proof of payment a few days before her release.
But it was another bail agent, who was not affiliated with LIS, that got her out of detention - after her friends raised even more money to hire another company.
"I was losing it inside there," Juarez recalled, using an expletive.
"I lost everything. When I was released I had nightmares I was back inside."
Libre Immigration Services never paid back her deposit, despite sending messages promising a refund. A spokesperson told the BBC that they would refund Juarez's bail amount once her friend verified their details.
Ankle monitors and debt
It is notoriously difficult for migrants like Juarez to make bail, which can be upwards of $7,000.
Once charged with illegal entry, a judge may grant bail, which allows the migrant to live freely while their case is heard, a process which can take years. Once a person's court case is completed, the bond amount is returned.
Bail agents, who are licensed to provide a down payment on bail and vouch that if the accused does not show up for court they will pay the rest, can help people get out of detention sooner. But many won't help migrants because they view them as too much of a flight risk. A 2024 government report found that a third of migrants not already in custody did not show up for court.
Libre by Nexus, also known as Nexus, was willing to take that risk.
Founded in 2013, its co-founders Michael Donovan and Richard Moore had served prison time in the 1990s and early 2000s for a string of fraud and forgery convictions.
Through his attorney, Donovan declined to comment. Moore did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
Although people with felony convictions are barred from holding a bond licence in many states, Nexus operated as a kind of middleman between immigrant clients and licensed bondsmen.
Holed up in detention in Louisiana after crossing the border, Rosa Murillo heard about Libre by Nexus from another inmate, and the 18-year-old Honduran's mother called them to arrange her $7,000 bail.
A Nexus employee picked her up and took her to a hotel room where she was told she would have to pay $420 a month and wear a GPS ankle monitor until her case was completed.
Federal regulators accused Nexus of implying, in their contracts, that the GPS bracelets were court-mandated, when they were actually the private company's requirement.
Murillo got a job as a waitress and tried to hide the ankle bracelet for fear that people might think she was a violent criminal.
Over the course of a decade, Libre by Nexus enabled more than 20,000 migrants like Murillo to be released on bail - and took in more than $230m in revenue, court documents show.
But the ankle bracelets were a constant source of annoyance for Nexus clients released from detention, according to two former employees who spoke to the BBC.
A former Nexus co-owner, Evan Ajin, told the BBC that the company stopped requiring released detainees to wear ankle bracelets in 2018.
But Mark Supetran, who was based in the Philippines and worked for the company for a few months in 2022, says the bracelets were still in use when he worked for the company.
Supetran said he would field 80 calls a day from people who were either going through the process themselves or were the loved one of someone who was. Telling them they would have to wear a tag on release was part of the conversation.
"Part of the script was to say something like: 'The client will be wearing an ankle monitor.' So that got me thinking, like, why?" he recalled. "It doesn't make sense, we're not the government."
Not getting refunds of bail deposits was another complaint. Another former employee told the BBC he was instructed to tell callers that they would get their money back once their case was completed.
"But that that was never the case," he told the BBC. "I mean, you had people calling me in almost every day like 'Hey, am I gonna get my money back? Am I gonna get my money back?'"
Ajin, the former Nexus co-owner, told the BBC that the contract clearly stated that monthly fees did not go towards their bond, but were programme fees, and so they could issue no refund.
The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), an agency created to stop predatory lending and other abusive financial practices, successfully sued Libre by Nexus and its parent company.
The lawsuit accused the firm of running a "predatory immigrant-services scam" that trapped victims into paying high, long-term fees. Nexus also misrepresented and concealed the terms, the lawsuit alleged, such as the non-refundable, monthly payments.
The judgment sided with the CFPB and a federal judge found the company liable for using predatory tactics against its clients in 2024, fining Nexus, its parent company, Ajin, Donovan and Moore $811m.
In addition to the hefty fine, the judge forbade the company from collecting on past debts.
Days after the 2024 order, Donovan sold a number of the company's assets, including customer lists and records - for $3.50.
As part of the agreement the buyer would also take on its debt.
Ajin says he ceased contact with everyone involved following the sale.
Moore is now in prison, after being convicted of filing fraudulent Nexus taxes. He and Donovan, who is also behind bars, are awaiting sentencing for insurance fraud and conspiracy. Donovan has also been charged with sexually abusing a boy under 12, but has not entered a plea in that case.
Business as usual
The purchaser of Nexus's assets was a Pennsylvania businessman named Vincent Smith, who had been sentenced to 10 months' probation in 2015 for conspiring with employees to write over $2m in fake bail bonds.
Smith called the new business Libre Immigration Services.
This March, the judge who issued the fine also ruled the sale of the company had violated her order by transferring the debts.
Judge Elizabeth Dillon voided the sale, but did not shut Libre Immigration Services down. She is due to review claims that LIS also violated the order by trying to build an app to collect debts from Nexus's old clients.
A former paralegal at Nexus, who went on to work for LIS, told the BBC about the app. She said after the sale, the lines between the two companies were blurred.
Another employee confirmed her account independently to the BBC, noting that the app was never finished because they could not obtain the client data.
A hearing date has not been set, and LIS has denied any wrongdoing, noting the company was never in possession of the client lists.
Libre Immigration Services continues to solicit immigrant clients and advertises its services online and on social media.
Its website features glossy photos of beaming families alongside the promise to "get your loved one released from a detention centre today!".
That wasn't Janie Aviles's experience. She had wired Libre Immigration Services $10,000 to help get her friend out of detention in Texas. But LIS did not pay his bail, Aviles said, until a month later, leaving him, like Juarez, in limbo.
When she called they offered various explanations and then stopped answering the telephone, she said.
Eventually she drove to the office listed on the website, which had shown a picture of LIS's logo hanging above the door. But on arrival, she found there was no storefront with the business's name and logo anywhere.
She said the company finally paid the bail a month after getting the funds, after she had reported them to the district attorney. No charges have been laid.
An LIS spokesperson said that "verification of significant information had to occur to prevent or minimise loss".
"The application was ultimately approved, and the cash bond was pledged to ICE. Presumably any delay related to the substantial bond amount and the heightened requirements of review."
They also said the office at that location was for business operations, and not client services, and that a sign had been ordered and would be installed, pending permits.
But the ordeal was enough to anger Aviles, who feared for her friend while he was stuck in detention. "I'm like 'This ain't right.'"

noticias.titulo: ANC fights to keep control of South Africa's key cities after election setback
noticias.resumen: The ANC appears reluctant to replicate its national power-sharing deal with the pro-business DA at the local level.
noticias.texto:
ANC fights to keep control of South Africa's key cities after election setback
- Published
The party that has dominated South Africa for more than 30 years is in a race against time to secure power-sharing deals in most of the country's cities after a massive drop in its support in this month's local elections.
The African National Congress (ANC) suffered its worstâ¯result since it came to power in 1994 when South Africa transitioned from the racist apartheid system to democracy.
It won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo, down from six in the last elections. It won the most votes in just two of the country's eight cities, compared with six in 2021.
At the national level, the ANC is sharing power with its long-time rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), but while there is still no official announcement, it appears that ANC party officials do not want to replicate this at the local level.
Parties have until 27 November to negotiate and form local governments.
What happened in the local election?
While the ANC saw a massive decline in its support, it still got more votes than any other party, 31%, down from the 46% in the last local election.
But in the country's economic powerhouse, Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg and Pretoria, the picture is different. The pro-business DA got the most votes in both cities, as well as the province's other main region, Ekurhuleni.
Nationally, the party got 25% of the vote, up from 22% five years ago.
It also retained its majority in its power base of Cape Town, and got the most votes in Nelson Mandela Bay, where Gqeberha (Port Elizabeth) is located.
The left-leaning uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party, led by former President Jacob Zuma, came third, with 10% of the vote. This is a repeat of its performance in the 2024 national election, when it came in third and became the official opposition after the DA joined the coalition government.
It emerged as the biggest party in KwaZulu-Natal province, which includes the port city of Durban, securing 34% of the vote. However, this leaves it reliant on agreeing a coalition with other parties.
The only party to secure an overall majority in a city was the DA in Cape Town.
Why is the ANC apparently choosing smaller parties over the DA?
The DA and ANC have had an uneasy alliance since they entered a coalition, along with eight other political parties, in 2024.
The two, long-standing rivals due to their opposing policies, were forced into an agreement after the ANC lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since the end of apartheid. This became known as the Government of National Unity (GNU).
Despite this, the two parties have continued to disagree on key issues, and both sides have threatened to rip up their power-sharing deal.
Ahead of the local elections, analysts predicted that the two parties could team up at municipal level, mirroring the national arrangement.
The ANC seems to have rejected this, with state broadcaster SABC reporting that most of the party's top leaders see an agreement with the DA as a last resort.
Instead, the party has been courting smaller parties to try and form councils in South Africa's cities.
In Gauteng, numerous reports point to an arrangement between the party and the anti-immigrant ActionSA, which emerged as the third largest party in the province with 17%, leaving it as a potential kingmaker.
The DA has also been trying to reach arrangements with smaller parties, and the ANC, but looks set to assume the opposition benches at least in Gauteng.
ActionSA is unlikely to work with the DA as they cannot agree on the mayoral candidates in Johannesburg and Pretoria.
Does this signal a breakdown in the relationship between the ANC and DA nationally?
It's too early to tell. Neither the ANC nor DA have spoken publicly about the future of their arrangement on a national level amid the ongoing coalition talks but the ANC's reluctance to partner with the DA in key cities points to continued strain between the two.
While the GNU has remained intact since it was formed in 2024, there have been those in the ANC who have been angered by what they view as the DA's dual role as opposition and partner in the coalition government and have pushed for the arrangement to end.
A party insider told the Daily Maverick on Sunday that a nationwide agreement to work with the DA at municipal level "was overwhelmingly rejected" at a meeting held by ANC members.
While some experts predict that the DA may have to consider its position in the coalition government given the ANC's stance, political analyst Andre Duvenhage told the BBC there was a possibility that "a lot of asymmetrical coalitions" could emerge - parties working together in one area and being in opposition elsewhere.
Another political analyst, Sandile Swana, said that any party wanting to leave the GNU over the failure to secure deals locally would be "[shooting] yourself in the foot".
Would coalition governments improve services?
This is what voters want.
The decline in the ANC's support was seen as being mainly due to high levels of corruption and a loss of confidence in its ability to provide basic services, such as electricity, water and rubbish collection.
While some attribute the increase backing for the DA to its record of competent management in municipalities under its control, some have accused it of neglecting poorer areas and townships.
But the experience of coalition governments over the past 10 years does not inspire much confidence that things will improve.
Half of the country's cities have been governed through power-sharing agreements since 2016 and these types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic.
As agreements collapse and new ones are forged, the delivery of basic services has often been affected.
This has been particularly evident in Gauteng, where governance in all three cities has come under scrutiny in recent years partly because of unstable governments.
Experts agree that even after new arrangements take effect, it will take longer than a five-year term to resolve the issues facing many municipalities, particularly South Africa's biggest city Johannesburg.
"I think if we are really turning the ship around, we are talking about a 10-year period," Duvenhage said.
Swana echoed this, saying it would take a decade to "cleanse and purify" local councils and "reinstate them as "proper municipalities".

noticias.titulo: Dead pets were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream
noticias.resumen: Grieving Filipinos confront a distressing reality: their dogs and cats may not have received the send-off they paid for.
noticias.texto:
Dead pets were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream
- Published
The livestream begins.
A man â bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses â walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of plastic-wrapped objects that spill out of the tall grass.
Names are written on the packages â Brandon; Ira; Lucky; Sweet â and numbers. One says 29kg (4.5 stone). Another says 2.5kg. Through the plastic you can make out what appears to be fur, claws and a flattened ear.
It's a mass dumping, the man explains. "We have about 25 animals here that have been dumped in bags. A couple of cats, some dogs."
"Purebreds," says the woman filming.
Warning: This story contains images some might find upsetting
In the weeks since that video was streamed on Facebook, Chris and Geraldine Taylor, who run animal rescue NGO Luna and Furry Siblings (LAFS), say they have uncovered 15 dumping sites in the suburbs of Bulacan, near the Philippines' capital of Manila.
In total they've unearthed the remains of some 170 dead pets. Belgian Malinois, golden retrievers, pugs, puppies and cats have been found dumped off service roads, sealed in septic tanks, floating in rivers and buried in vacant lots.
Many of these animals are thought to have been sent to cremation businesses in the expectation they would be turned to ash.
Now, many grieving owners are having to confront a distressing reality: their beloved pets may not have received the send-off they paid for. The urn in their home may not contain their pet at all. And they may in fact see their so-called fur child again, jettisoned like common waste on the side of a highway.
One saw the livestream and wrote on Facebook: "I think one of those pets is mine." Below, they attached a photo of a beaming Alsatian.
170 carcasses found
When Chris arrived on that back road three weeks ago, he couldn't have known he was uncorking a scandal that would see at least one business reportedly shut, four people placed under investigation, and a personal invite to sit down with a senator to discuss animal-cruelty laws.
Chris, a former police officer, and his wife are retired, but only formally. For the past three years, they've been running an animal rescue shelter out of their home in San Jose del Monte, 30km (18.6 miles) north-east of central Manila.
On 30 October, he'd driven into town to report a case of animal neglect at the local district office. When he arrived, he was told the official in charge had just left to respond to another complaint: a report of dumped animals on a nearby roadside.
Chris had seen this once before: 14 dogs that were found and soon reburied. This time, he followed the official to the scene and started documenting â taking photos, scanning the bodies for microchips and uploading footage to his Facebook page.
"I figured there's got to be more to this," he explains. "So we put out word: if anybody knows anything, any other dump locations... just report it. Let us know."
In the days that followed, tip-offs started trickling in. More dumpsites emerged.
"The long vacant lot on the left side... that's where the smell comes from," read one message.
"When we ran to this place it smelled of rotting animals," read another, accompanied by a photo of a map with a location circled in red.
By crowdsourcing intel in this way, and collaborating with authorities, LAFS has so far uncovered a total of 15 dumpsites, containing an estimated 170 animals. "Some of them were just bags of bones," Chris says. "Others were liquefied."
LAFS has meticulously documented the crime scenes. Often wearing little more for protection than an N95 mask and rubber gloves, Chris crouches in the underbrush and slices open discarded plastic bags, picking through the contents while Geraldine holds the camera.
Their Facebook videos have racked up more than 30 million views. Commenters ask Chris if he has seen their pet among the bodies, or if he can turn a carcass over so they can check for identifying marks.
Some are successful. On that first night in October, all 25 bodies were returned to their owners.
There's a question which hangs uncomfortably over every dumpsite: who would do something like this?
As more owners came forward, a common denominator emerged. Many said they'd taken the animals to be incinerated at the same place: a crematorium called Ahjay Paws in the city of Bacoor, not far from Manila.
"So I posted: anybody that's had Ahjay's services... these might be your animals," says Chris. "And man, it just flooded in."
'God knows what was inside those urns'
The Philippines has long been a dog-loving nation, but since the Covid-19 pandemic the "fur parenting" community has exploded.
A 2021 study found the country had the highest rate of dog ownership in the Asia-Pacific. Since then, the pet dog population has increased 4.7% year on year, according to another study, exceeding 21 million in 2025.
As the numbers soar, businesses have stepped up to address an inevitable implication: more deaths.
"Cremation here in the Philippines has become quite a big thing with the boom of the pet industry," says Anna Cabrera, director at the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (Paws). "There's even a ceremony where they hold wakes for the pets."
These events offer grieving owners a last chance to see their beloved pets before they're taken to a crematorium and transmuted into an urnful of ashes.
Or not, as the case may be.
Revecca Calling, who lives south of Bulacan in the city of Cavite, says she paid Ahjay Paws 8,500 Philippine pesos (Â£100; $133) to cremate her dog Olaf in January. The price was calculated according to weight, and included a 30-minute viewing where she could say her final goodbye.
Calling says Ahjay Paws told her they couldn't record the cremation, as it might endanger the staff. They took away Olaf's body, and a few days later handed back a small urn that purportedly contained her cremated remains.
When nine months later Calling heard that dozens of animals' bodies had been found dumped on an empty plot of land, potentially at the behest of a pet cremation business, she was devastated.
"Pet owners entrust these services with something very important: the remains of a beloved family member," she says. "We need to know what happened."
Earlier this month, the Philippines' National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) filed criminal complaints against four individuals in connection with dumped pets. Among them is the owner of Ahjay Paws and two people who ran Bulacan's Pet HPHT Crematory.
According to the NBI, Ahjay Paws had initially arranged to acquire a cremation machine from Pet HPHT â but when it didn't arrive, they opted to send the pet remains to Pet HPHT instead. When the volume of those remains became more than Pet HPHT could handle, that firm paid a third party to bury them.
One interpretation is that the dumping incidents are a result of logistical failures: two businesses that bit off more than they could chew and took desperate measures to make the problem go away.
But there's another theory: that the dead pets could be evidence of a lucrative racket, with people's money taken to incinerate their pets but the animals then being dumped instead.
There is a word for this kind of deception in Philippine law â estafa; where a perpetrator knowingly misleads a victim to financially defraud them â and the NBI say they are investigating it as a possibility in this case.
Two weeks ago, Ahjay Paws' owner denied responsibility for the dumping in San Jose del Monte, according to local media. The company is apparently no longer operating, and the BBC has been unable to contact it.
The BBC has also reached out to Pet HPHT and invited it to respond. On Facebook, the firm said the dumping allegations were "completely false and have no basis".
Another grieving pet owner, Emelia Legada, says she paid Ahjay Paws 10,000 Philippine pesos (Â£120; $160) to cremate her dog Harvey six months ago.
"I just can't accept the pain of not knowing what might have happened to him," she says. "I really want to confirm whether Harvey was properly cremated, and whether the ashes I received were truly his."
Many are wrestling with the same uncertainty. As Cabrera puts it: "God knows what that was inside those urns."
In response to those anxieties, a veterinarian in nearby Quezon City has started offering complimentary forensic ash testing. For those whose pets have been found among the bodies, other crematoriums have offered to do the job properly, and for free.
The animal welfare society, Paws, is volunteering legal services to help people file complaints with the authorities, and has received more than 150 requests so far. It is also calling for a nationwide audit of all pet cremation businesses.
Animal-cruelty law 'doesn't apply'
On 2 November, Percival Vilar CendaÃ±a of the Philippines' progressive Akbayan Party appeared on national television. He was there to speak about the pet-dumping scandal, which, in the span of a few days, had flared into a national disgrace.
"Our worst fears have been confirmed," he told the Bilyonaryo news channel. "Now we see that these are not isolated incidents. It is true that this is a syndicate that is conducting widespread operations."
Neither the police nor the NBI have confirmed that the dumpings were carried out by a "syndicate", nor that they were "widespread". Many details surrounding the case remain murky. But the hysteria is real â and CendaÃ±a was giving voice to a common sentiment.
"Those who deceived these poor fur parents should be jailed," he said.
At least three individuals have surrendered to the NBI and been charged with violating the city's Code of Sanitation, the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act, and the Sanitation Code of the Philippines.
But many feel this doesn't go far enough, and say it fails to hold anyone liable for the way the animals' remains were treated.
Cabrera says the country's animal-cruelty law doesn't cover the treatment of animals after death. And "there's no crime if there's no law".
The scandal has prompted a groundswell to change that. Lawmakers like CendaÃ±a are pushing for a national commission on animal welfare to ensure their dignity in life and death.
Meanwhile, Cabrera says Paws will seek "moral and exemplary" damages on behalf of aggrieved pet owners.
One woman whose dog was suspected to have been found among the dumped bodies told the BBC she couldn't speak about it because she was "feeling weak".
"I haven't slept for three days from all the crying," she said.
Chris has also been losing sleep, taking calls from grieving pet owners who have watched his videos. "Hundreds of people call me in tears, just sobbing," he says.
"They're in so much pain. And half the time you're telling them: 'you're not going to find your pet. It's been too long; we're not going to be able to identify it.' And it just crushes them."
As well as new laws, Chris wants stricter enforcement of existing rules. He wants to know how he managed to unearth so much in the space of a fortnight, and why people keep coming to him saying they don't trust the police to take their concerns seriously, he says.
The BBC contacted Philippine National Police (PNP) for comment, but didn't hear back. Earlier this month, PNP chief Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr said authorities were determined to hold accountable those who allegedly took advantage of grieving pet owners, saying such exploitation "must be addressed with the full force of the law", according to ABS-CBN.
"Fraud is not measured solely by the amount of money taken, but also by the damage inflicted on the people whose trust has been betrayed," Nartatez said.
"To the affected pet owners, we recognise the pain and distress this incident has caused your families."
Yet the police themselves have come under official scrutiny.
On Monday, the National Police Commission announced an investigation into officers in Cavite and Bulacan after they suggested LAFS might be involved in the pet dumping because they were often first on the scene. The officers did not present evidence for their claims. The investigation also covers reports that officers visited the Taylors' home and took photographs.
Meanwhile, countless grieving pet owners are suspended in purgatory: desperate for closure on what happened to their dogs and cats, and calling on authorities to do more.
"We want the case to be properly investigated and those responsible to be held accountable," says Calling.â¯ "I believe that no secret remains hidden forever."
Legada, for her part, says: "I just want to find out what really happened to Harvey and where his remains are. I want to know whether he was properly cremated."
She also wants people to know: "You can't trust anyone these days."
With additional reporting by Virma Simonette Rivera

noticias.titulo: A new Nepal, an old neighbour - Balendra Shah's India test
noticias.resumen: Trade, connectivity and regional cooperation will be on top of the agenda when Nepal's PM meets his India counterpart.
noticias.texto:
A new Nepal, an old neighbour - Balendra Shah's India test
- Published
Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India has raised hopes of a reset, marking the first high-level engagement between leaders of Nepal's new political generation and its giant neighbour.
It is Shah's first bilateral visit since his Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) swept to power in March, six months after a Gen Z uprising against corruption and nepotism toppled K P Sharma Oli's government.
The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, during which he will meet his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi and other senior officials.
The talks are expected to cover a broad range of issues, including economic and energy cooperation, the opening of new air corridors, and a reconstruction assistance package following the devastating flash floods that struck Nepal in August.
The disaster killed more than 1,450 in the Himalayan nation, while thousands remain missing and unaccounted for.
India and Nepal share close ethnic, cultural, religious and economic ties, with a largely open border stretching more than 1,750km (1,080 miles).
Wedged between India and China, Nepal is a strategic buffer and, analysts say, its stability has direct implications for India's security.
But over the decades the relationship has been strained by territorial disputes, allegations of political interference and resentment over what many in Nepal see as the dominant 'Big Brother' attitude of Delhi.
Nevertheless, analysts see Shah's visit as an opportunity for a reset.
"The new Nepali leadership says they do not have the political baggage of the past and they want to focus on development, diplomacy and economic partnership," Ranjit Rae, a former Indian ambassador to Nepal tells BBC.
"They seem to be more pragmatic, less ideological. I personally feel it's an optimistic moment," he adds.
Since Nepal abolished monarchy and became a democratic republic in 2008 three political parties dominated the governance.
Delhi has maintained close contacts with all of them â the Communist Party of Nepal (CPN â UML), the Nepali Congress and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre).
Nepal's communist parties were seen as closer to India's rival China, owing to ideological ties, and often criticised Delhi over what they viewed as unequal bilateral agreements.
Due to Nepal's strategic location, both Delhi and Beijing compete for influence in Kathmandu, leading to accusations the two Asian giants are meddling in the internal affairs of Nepal.
But Nepal's ties with India extend beyond diplomacy and strategic interests.
The Hindu-majority nations share deep social ties, with families straddling the open border and communities interacting daily.
Bilateral trade exceeds $9bn, heavily skewed in India's favour - a longstanding source of resentment in Kathmandu. India is also Nepal's main supplier of petroleum products and several food items, and a key transit route for its trade with the rest of the world.
One key area of co-operation is hydropower. India has approved projects to import up to 1,200MW of electricity from Nepal and is looking to expand imports further.
"India has a huge demand for electricity and Nepal has the potential to generate due to its water resources and geography. It's not just bilateral, Nepal also exports electricity to Bangladesh via India," says Rae.
India has often been among the first countries to assist Nepal during major natural disasters, including the 2015 earthquake and the flash floods in August this year.
Despite the close links, Nepal and India have their differences.
In 2019, Nepal was furious after India published a map that included areas claimed by Kathmandu, in a western region close to the border with China, as part of its territory. That raised heightened awareness in Kathmandu about the region.
The diplomatic wrangle escalated after Nepal published its own map which included those disputed areas.
"I hope Nepal's prime minister raises the border issue with Delhi this time. There may not be a resolution immediately, but they should start negotiations to settle the issue," Kanak Mani Dixit, a veteran Nepali political analyst, told the BBC.
Nepal has also long urged India to open additional air entry routes, allowing large aircraft to fly in from the west to its new airports at Bhairahawa, near the Buddhist holy site of Lumbini, and Pokhara, a major tourist destination.
Access to Indian airspace would mean shorter flights at lower cost and, with more flights, the airports would become commercially viable.
Some in Nepal also believe that Delhi is wary of the fact that the Gautam Buddha international airport was constructed by China's Northwest Civil Aviation Airport and the airport in Pokhara was built with Chinese financial assistance.
Shah has yet to make any overtures to Beijing, but sent a 20-member delegation of party MPs to China for an 11-day visit from 15 November, ahead of his trip to India - seen as an effort to balance ties with Nepal's two powerful neighbours.
Shah had pledged not to travel abroad during his first year in office, but devastating flash floods in August have changed the calculus.
His government estimates reconstruction will cost nearly $5bn, while international aid pledged so far has fallen short of expectations.
But some observers in Nepal believe that Shah's preparations for the high-stake India visit have been less than thorough.
"Prime Minister Shah and his advisors are young and fresh, but they do lack experience. Repeatedly they have exhibited a lack of gravitas in governance, which would be essential for diplomacy with an overwhelmingly powerful neighbour," says Dixit.
Shah is already facing criticism over some of his government's recent decisions, including to remove police chief Dan Bahadur from his post after he allegedly refused to comply with directives from the Prime Minister's office.
Police were sent to some news organisations to detain journalists for their news coverage triggering accusations of curtailing press freedom.
While Kathmandu has ambitions in advancing its ties with India, the real test for Shah would be to return home with tangible outcomes. Securing concrete commitments from Delhi on financial aid would be seen as a diplomatic success and could help blunt growing domestic criticism.

noticias.titulo: Trump calls for Nvidia to reinstate ‘brilliant’ Jensen Huang
noticias.resumen: US president calls tech giant to give former CEO 'a second chance' and urges him to 'make a big apology'.
noticias.texto:
Trump calls for Nvidia to reinstate ‘brilliant’ Jensen Huang
US president calls tech giant to give former CEO ‘a second chance’ and urges him to ‘make a big apology’.
US President Donald Trump has said he would welcome Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s CEO, more than a week after the company’s founder stepped down over a scandal involving extramarital affairs.
“You have one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world, and where is he going to go?” Trump told reporters on Friday. “I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance.”
Trump also described Jensen Huang as “a good man” who “made some bad decisions”.
“I’d like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back, because he created something with Blackwell,” Trump said, referring to Nvidia’s most advanced chips.
Huang resigned on November 12, following media reports of an intimate relationship with an alleged spy for Beijing who may have helped route restricted chips to China. US intelligence officials are said to have previously known about the possible espionage link.
Two more affairs have since been reported. The New York Times reported on Friday that the suspected spy, Alice Huang, has extensive ties to China’s defence industry through her family and associates.
Trump also appeared to contradict Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who had said earlier on Friday that Jensen Huang did not come up in talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.
“I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, ‘Oh, brilliant, brilliant! He’s a brilliant man,'” said Trump of his meeting with the Chinese president.
No way back
In a post on X on Tuesday, Jensen Huang offered to return to the company.
However, Nvidia’s board has ruled out his comeback. Board chairperson Harvey Jones said on an earnings call later that day that the directors unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation and do not plan to reinstate him.
The scandal has also drawn in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Republican Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas told The Wall Street Journal that Lutnick had repeatedly ignored warnings about AI chips being smuggled to China before the scandal broke, though he stopped short of calling for the commerce secretary’s resignation.
Trump said he still supported Lutnick.
“I have not lost confidence,” Trump said, calling Lutnick “a different kind of a guy, very good businessman”.
Democrats, who will take control of Congress in January, are investigating whether Lutnick used his office to help Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm run by his sons, avoid losses tied to scrutiny of Nvidia’s links to a Chinese company.

noticias.titulo: Can Africa’s new credit rating agency change how the continent is assessed?
noticias.resumen: The new African agency aims to bring greater transparency to credit ratings.
noticias.texto:
Can Africa’s new credit rating agency change how the continent is assessed?
The new African agency aims to bring greater transparency to credit ratings.
Abuja, Nigeria – On October 7, the African Union officially launched the Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA), bringing to fruition an initiative first endorsed by African leaders in 2017.
The agency, based in Port Louis, Mauritius, is designed to provide independent assessments of African governments and corporate borrowers, drawing on local data and expertise to complement ratings issued by international agencies. Its first sovereign ratings are expected by the end of March.
Its interim chief executive, Sifiso Falala, says AfCRA is already in discussions with 15 African governments with research planned in countries that include Mauritius, Kenya, Togo, the Seychelles and Burundi.
The case for AfCRA rests partly on the cost of how African economies are perceived by financial markets. A 2023 study by the United Nations Development Programme estimated that subjectivities in sovereign credit ratings cost African countries $74.5bn through excessive interest payments and foregone lending.
African governments have long argued that international rating methodologies do not adequately account for the continent’s economic structures and circumstances.
The major international agencies – Moody’s, S&P Global Ratings and Fitch Ratings – have disputed suggestions that their assessments systematically disadvantage African borrowers. At a Chatham House discussion in June, Moody’s Marie Diron argued that the agency’s analysis of four decades of global sovereign default data showed that African countries with a particular rating had broadly the same probability of default as equally rated borrowers elsewhere.
For example, she said, a sovereign with a B rating had an estimated one-year default probability of about 5 percent regardless of whether it was African or from another region.
That is an important counterargument. AfCRA’s challenge will not simply be to produce different ratings but to demonstrate that its assessments are more comprehensive, transparent and predictive of actual credit risk. Its credibility will ultimately depend on the evidence behind its conclusions, including when those conclusions are unfavourable to African borrowers.
Transparency and mutual learning
For Falala, the agency’s priority is to ensure that assessments better reflect the economic realities of African countries.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, he said: “A significant number of African countries carry speculative-grade ratings despite having no history of sovereign default.
“This raises legitimate questions about whether prevailing models adequately capture African economic realities. We believe our analytical framework can contribute to a constructive reassessment of these assumptions, encouraging the entire industry to examine whether the indicators used to determine creditworthiness remain relevant, proportionate and sufficiently predictive of actual default risk.”
Falala said the agency was not seeking more favourable ratings for African borrowers but greater accuracy through engagement with established rating agencies.
“Our objective is not to manufacture better ratings for Africa, but to produce more accurate ratings of Africa in collaboration with established rating agencies. Importantly, we believe that a stronger AfCRA will contribute to a stronger credit rating industry overall,” he said.
That distinction will be central to the agency’s credibility. An institution established partly in response to dissatisfaction with existing ratings must demonstrate that its own assessments are independent of political pressure and the interests of the governments and companies it evaluates.
Falala acknowledged the scepticism surrounding the industry, saying AfCRA has an opportunity to rebuild confidence through transparency and analytical independence. He said the agency was not seeking confrontation with established rating providers but saw considerable scope for collaboration and mutual learning.
More local data and methodologies
Beyond sovereign ratings, AfCRA intends to assess companies, municipalities, banks and local-currency debt. This broader coverage could address gaps in information about borrowers that receive limited attention from international agencies while providing domestic investors with additional assessments of credit risk.
The potential benefits extend beyond the ratings themselves. African pension funds, banks and other institutional investors need reliable information to assess domestic borrowers and allocate capital. More comprehensive coverage, supported by stronger local data, could help reduce information gaps and support the development of domestic capital markets.
However, additional ratings will not automatically translate into cheaper borrowing. Their influence will depend on whether investors consider the assessments credible and useful in making investment decisions.
Abdussalam Muazu, an associate chartered economist at the Institute of Chartered Economists of Nigeria, said limited information about African borrowers has contributed to the uncertainty investors factor into lending decisions.
“African governments and companies often pay more to borrow than their ratings suggest, partly because investors know too little about them and price in the uncertainty.
“The big agencies have few analysts on the ground, and much of Africa’s economy runs through informal trade, mobile money and community finance that is hard to measure from outside. An African agency can bring local knowledge into credit ratings and help build the data that is missing today, which gives investors less reason to charge for guesswork,” he told Al Jazeera.
The argument points to a wider problem: The availability and quality of economic data can shape how creditworthiness is assessed. Informal economic activity, for example, is not always adequately captured in conventional indicators, even though it contributes significantly to livelihoods and economic activity across the continent.
Methodology is another part of the debate. Different approaches to assessing sovereign risk can produce different conclusions about the same country’s ability and willingness to meet its financial obligations. AfCRA, therefore, will need to explain clearly how its models account for factors that may be overlooked or insufficiently reflected in existing assessments.
Dayo Obisan, a financial market professional, told Al Jazeera that African countries need rating methodologies that better reflect their economic circumstances and their access to capital.
“The compelling question is how does Africa ensure its peculiarities are factored into the determination of its perception as a sovereign and its access to much-needed capital, which rides on this perception?”
He said an African rating institution could bring greater understanding of these circumstances through its presence across the continent, improved data and methodologies that complement existing approaches.
“The value proposition for the creation of an Africa-focused credit rating agency centres on richer local data, contextual insight, wider coverage and support for domestic markets,” Obisan said.
Independence and credibility under scrutiny
But local knowledge alone will not be enough. AfCRA will also have to demonstrate that its methodology is rigorous, consistent and transparent and its ratings can withstand scrutiny from investors beyond the continent.
Its ownership and financing arrangements will also be important. The agency describes itself as privately owned and self-funded while its planned sovereign assessments will operate on a solicited basis, meaning governments pay for ratings and provide access to officials and financial information.
This is a model also used by established rating agencies, but it makes safeguards against conflicts of interest particularly important. The African Union says governments may not own shares in AfCRA, but the agency will still need to demonstrate that commercial relationships with the borrowers it assesses cannot influence its analytical decisions.
Ultimately, AfCRA’s credibility will not be determined by how many African countries it rates or how far its assessments differ from those of Moody’s, S&P and Fitch.
It will depend on whether investors trust its analyses, whether its methodology withstands scrutiny and, above all, whether it can remain independent when its findings are politically inconvenient.
Its defining test may come when an African government rejects an unfavourable assessment and the agency refuses to change it.
As Falala put it, “What strengthens AfCRA should ultimately strengthen the credibility of the entire credit rating industry. Africa needs more credible assessments, not competing narratives.”

noticias.titulo: Denmark expels Russian diplomat over alleged plot to kill Ukrainian rapper
noticias.resumen: Copenhagen accuses Moscow of planning assassination with banned local gang; Russia says no evidence for allegation.
noticias.texto:
Denmark expels Russian diplomat over alleged plot to kill Ukrainian rapper
Copenhagen accuses Moscow of planning assassination with banned local gang; Russia says no evidence for allegation.
Denmark has said it is expelling Russia’s defence attaché after accusing Moscow intelligence of plotting to kill a Ukrainian rapper at a concert near Copenhagen.
“We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attaché from Denmark” within seven days, Danish Minister for Foreign Affairs Lars Lokke Rasmussen told a news conference on Friday.
Denmark is also considering suspending Schengen visas for Russians, he added.
The expulsion ultimatum comes hours after Denmark’s intelligence agency, PET, said it suspected Russia of planning the assassination during a concert in a Copenhagen suburb with help of a Danish gang.
Danish public broadcaster DR named the rapper as Kyivstoner, who has both Ukrainian and US citizenship.
“A Russian assassination attempt is not something we’ve seen in Denmark before, and that gives me an impression of an increasingly aggressive and risk-taking Russia,” PET head Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen told journalists on Friday.
“The case shows, in our assessment, that the Russian intelligence services attempted to carry out an execution in Denmark,” he said.
Thwarted plot
According to PET, three people were stopped in a car near the music venue where the rapper was scheduled to perform on September 25. Police found firearms and knives in the vehicle.
Two people were placed under formal investigation on Friday for attempted murder and for helping a foreign intelligence service operate in Denmark. Police and PET suspect Loyal to Familia, a street gang and criminal network banned since 2021, helped plan the attack.
Police and intelligence services made their announcements as two Danish men appeared in court near Copenhagen on Friday, charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and attempted murder, court documents showed.
According to the court documents, the suspects were arrested five minutes before the concert was set to begin and one of them had bought a ticket to the performance. The concert was cancelled.
Exchange of reactions
In response to Friday’s announcement, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said, “We are facing a cornered Russia, acting more aggressively and with a greater propensity to take risks.” The strongest response would be to “not waver” and to keep supporting Ukraine, she added.
European Council President Antonio Costa said the alleged assassination attempt was “unacceptable” and “will not go unanswered”. He promised Denmark the European Union’s full backing against what he called Russian hybrid attacks.
Russia’s Foreign Ministry spokeswoman, Maria Zakharova, said Moscow would give “an appropriate response”, Russia’s state news agency TASS reported. The Russian embassy in Copenhagen called the expulsion “vengeful” and said Denmark had not presented “any evidence of Russia’s involvement in this mysterious crime”.
Copenhagen has accused Moscow of other hybrid attacks, which are acts short of open war, such as sabotage and disruption. In September 2025, drones shut down Copenhagen airport for hours, in what Denmark called a hybrid attack.
PET said in September that Russia was recruiting Danish citizens to help plan sabotage against Danish defence firms with ties to Ukraine.
Russia has denied involvement in such operations.

noticias.titulo: Can Mauricio Pochettino save Man United from Premier League relegation?
noticias.resumen: Mauricio Pochettino will take charge of Manchester United for the first time on Sunday, in a trip to rivals Liverpool.
noticias.texto:
Can Mauricio Pochettino save Man United from Premier League relegation?
Mauricio Pochettino will take charge of Manchester United for the first time on Sunday, in a trip to rivals Liverpool.
Manchester United will be led by a third manager in three years when Mauricio Pochettino takes charge of his first match since replacing Michael Carrick.
The fact that the Premier League clash is against their fierce rivals Liverpool – the team that, with United, are joint record English top-flight champions – is an added twist to a sordid recent tale for the Manchester club.
When Sir Alex Ferguson retired after lifting a then-record 20th league title in 2013, the Red Devils had climbed to the biggest and richest club in the world.
Now, apart from not being able to claim a Premier League crown since 2013, they are laden with debt – and worse still, they sit inside the relegation zone.
Can Pochettino save Man United from relegation?
The last time United were relegated from the top flight was in the 1973–1974 season. That came only six years after one of the club’s greatest nights – the lifting of the European Cup (now the Champions League), making them the first English club to do so.
Their fall this time around has not come quite as quickly, with their last crowning as European champions in 2008, and they have not been relegated – yet.
Few expect them to be. It would be unthinkable given the changed landscape of the entire footballing world, which has become awash with finances that clearly separate the elite and their resources from the rest.
When Pochettino was introduced to the media for the first time on Friday, the gathered press did not mention the word “relegation” even once.
So the simple answer is: yes, he can save the club from relegation. The longer equation is that the alternative would surely be the greatest shock in the history of a game famed for upsets and underdogs.
What problem does Pochettino need to solve first at United?
Words like identity, fitness, formation, and one that Pochettino awkwardly dropped on Friday, “philosophy”, have dogged every manager at Old Trafford since Ferguson’s departure.
“We arrived with the idea to create something from scratch, with our own philosophy and how we like to work,” Pochettino told the gathered reporters.
“We need to improve our players, find a way to perform, but the future and identity of the club is very clear.
“It is an historic club with an amazing years competing and being one of the best in the world.
“It is difficult to find another club that is the size of United. We need to be open-minded to do our best, and the players need to buy the idea that we need to improve.
“The job is to get the rest of the historic club, Manchester United, into a different place to where we are now.”
All of that can wait, because Liverpool are the next opponents, and for United, they do not come any bigger.
The Manchester derby has taken on a new level in recent years – although the tide there may also soon turn, depending on City’s appeal against their charges – but the rivalries against the Reds and Leeds United have the deepest roots for United fans.
A recent defeat to the revived latter still weighs heavily.
Pochettino needs to find a way for the team to start winning, and it needs to come soon. The club’s opening to the season is their worst since 1986, and one win – the worst return in the league – has left United just one point off bottom place.
By the time Pochettino and his United players walk out to the hostility of the Anfield crowd, they could be at the very foot of the table.
Will Pochettino change United’s formation?
The easiest part of the equation for Pochettino is the formation. With the United States national team, which he left to join United, the Argentinian deployed the 4-2-3-1 tactic that even Ferguson had evolved to in his final years.
Pochettino’s Tottenham, the club he made his managerial name with, were always set out in the same way with Harry Kane leading the line.
The United squad – which were moved to an uncomfortable 3-4-3 by Carrick’s predecessor, Ruben Amorim – are built for Pochettino’s style, but the task of melding them together had eluded Carrick and will be the key to their imminent return.
What long-term problems does Pochettino face at United?
The off-field troubles at United are well documented. The club are weighed down by the debts accrued with the Glazer family’s 2005 purchase.
Jim Ratcliffe’s investment three years ago has seen the Englishman and his INEOS group take control of footballing matters, but the annual interest the club pays remains a heavy burden.
The ownership is committed to its plan to rebuild the Old Trafford stadium to increase capacity and, with it, move the club to a more sustainable future.
That means the spending power that once saw United lead the way in transfer signings has diminished to the point where they cannot compete financially with Liverpool, City and Arsenal on the domestic front, let alone Spanish giants Real Madrid and Barcelona on the continent.
This is no easy fix for the manager or their owners, and is undoubtedly the long-term challenge for everyone involved.
What signings will Pochettino and United target in January transfer window?
Although the squad is set up for a 4-2-3-1 formation, they lack strength in depth.
Striker Benjamin Sesko has had an injury-plagued start to his United career since his move two seasons ago, and the Serbian international was far from the finished product when he arrived.
The 23-year-old’s absence this season has left a glaring hole up front, with Cameroon forward Bryan Mbeumo admirably leading the line with great endeavour, but lacking the presence a lone striker requires.
Despite needing a world-class finisher and being well stocked at the back, United have problems at the other end of the pitch, shipping 30 goals in all competitions this season.
Only two teams have conceded more than United’s 19 in the Premier League.
Luke Shaw’s availability at left-back has left United exposed in that position and made their failure to sign Lewis Hall in the summer all the more galling.
The Newcastle defender has since shone on international duty for England, and a move for the exciting 22-year-old in January seems the most obvious attempt United must make to appease their hugely unsettled fanbase.
What is Pochettino’s best Premier League finish?
Pochettino’s second-place finish with Tottenham in 2017 remains the North London club’s best league finish since 1962, only two years after their last top-flight title.
Will Pochettino be given enough time by United’s owners?
Pochettino will be the ninth manager to take charge of United in the last 13 seasons, and that does not include a further three interim coaches.
United fans never turn on their manager, and only recently, for the first time in the club’s history, have they turned on the players.
The same clearly cannot be said of the ownership.
It felt that Pochettino corrected his “philosophy” faux pas before he had finished that same answer on Friday. It was a word most associated with Louis van Gaal’s time at the club, and was rejected by players and fans alike.
United have an inbuilt philosophy and identity that buys players and managers time, built on attacking football and endless running.
The modern trend towards a high press should suit that mentality. To do that, Pochettino needs to unite the sleeping giants of Manchester. How long he will have to do so, based on the patience shown with his predecessors, is, however, anyone’s guess.

noticias.resumen: Police say two children among dead as search continues for more victims.
noticias.texto:
Overturned boat carrying mourners to funeral kills at least four in Nigeria
Police say two children among dead as search continues for more victims.
A boat believed to be carrying hundreds of people to a funeral has overturned in southern Nigeria, killing at least four people, according to police.
The overcrowded vessel capsized on Friday in Bayelsa State after a mechanical failure while travelling from the communities of Ayama to Ukubie, police spokesperson Musa Mohammed told the Reuters news agency.
He said the dead were two adults and two children.
Police said 24 people were rescued, with 19 treated at a local clinic, and five taken to a hospital in the state capital.
Search teams were still looking for more victims, police said. Police did not say how many people were on board, but some residents told Reuters there were at least 300.
Police said the driver fled and the vessel’s manager was taken into custody.
According to a statement from the Bayelsa State Police Command, the accident occurred at the river junction between the Oweikorogha and Otuan communities, in the state’s Southern Ijaw district.
The boat that capsized was travelling “for a burial ceremony”, the statement also said, adding that police are “coordinating efforts with local divers and other responders”.
Such boat accidents are common on Nigeria’s busy rivers and waterways, often caused by overloaded vessels, poor maintenance or failure to comply with safety regulations.
A similar incident occurred in August, when at least 51 died after a boat sank in northwest Nigeria’s Sokoto State, and another in January, when at least 26 people drowned after a boat ferrying people from Jigawa to Yobe State capsized.
